text:
Timing: 0:00–1:15.
Open with the outcome, not your résumé: ‘I joined Suno as a full-stack engineering intern. I completed my assigned project in three weeks, noticed that the recommendations were weak as a user, and asked to join a small, loosely formed recommendations effort. Over the next roughly eight weeks, I helped turn that open-ended problem into three production homepage feeds.’
Then establish your ownership precisely: ‘I owned every data pipeline, the rollout, and production health; I did most of the backend serving and frontend implementation; and I co-designed the architecture, ranking logic, and experiments with an ML scientist and a data scientist.’
Transition: ‘I’ll start with why this mattered at company scale, then explain the product and engineering decisions, including where my first approaches failed.’

text:
Timing: 1:15–3:20.
This slide is the five-minute impact requirement. Say: ‘These were not side-page experiments. They became the first discovery surfaces users encounter on the homepage.’
Explain the two strongest results: the creation-seeded treatment increased feed-specific playtime by 63%, while the personalized creator treatment increased net follows by 15% and was marked statistically significant after the team’s adjustment and bot filtering. Do not imply that these are absolute rates; they are relative lifts versus their controls.
The third number is scope: three live feeds built in parallel, across data, ranking, serving, UI, experiments, and rollout. If challenged on the For You result, say the exact quantitative readout was not included in the materials you brought; the offline treatment shipped after holding or improving engagement and improving the serving path. Do not manufacture a number.
Transition: ‘Those metrics mattered because Suno’s product loop is structurally different from a conventional streaming app.’

Timing: 3:20–5:15.
Make the product distinction concrete. Spotify or SoundCloud mostly infer preference from consumption. Suno has an additional, unusually strong signal: what a person tried to create. But that signal has special semantics—creations may be private, titles may be stylized, and a creator’s own work should not be treated exactly like public catalog content.
Tie the project to the company goal without overclaiming retention causality: ‘Retention was the company priority. These feeds targeted leading behaviors that support retention—qualified listening, creator follows, and repeat discovery. The experiments demonstrated those leading indicators; the internship window was too short to claim a fully measured long-term retention effect.’

Timing: 7:00–8:30.
This slide prevents two bad interpretations: that you only implemented someone else’s design, or that you are claiming to have invented the recommendation science alone.
Use this exact framing: ‘The ML scientist brought deeper judgment about recommendation algorithms, scoring, and metric interpretation. I brought the engineering ownership required to turn those ideas into reliable user-facing systems. I wrote every data pipeline, most of the serving and UI code, and I owned rollout and health. We co-owned architecture, ranking, and experimentation.’
Never say the scientist was a weak engineer. In an interview, that reads as poor leadership. Describe the complementary skill split and show that you made the team more effective.

text:
Timing: 8:30–10:20.
Explain the systems in product language before architecture. For You is a mixture feed: it can combine multiple signals and degrade gracefully to personal direct buckets or trends. Because You Create is an anchor feed: the exact creation that explains the shelf must survive and be visible. Creators You May Like recommends a different entity entirely—a person—and optimizes for follows rather than plays.
This distinction drove different retrieval spaces, ranking logic, cold-start behavior, hard floors, and fallbacks. It is a good depth signal because it shows you did not treat ‘recommendations’ as one generic model problem.
Transition: ‘I wanted those differences to live on one reusable platform so that a new product hypothesis did not require a new stack.’

name: arch-feedback
text: Every served item is attributable to its feed, position, source, and experiment.
textPreview: Every served item is attributable to its feed, position, source, and experiment.

text:
Timing: 10:20–13:20.
Walk left to right and keep internal names out. User behavior and content representations produce candidates. Candidate retrieval is intentionally broad; ranking and filtering decide what is safe and useful. Each feed then applies its own assembly semantics. Expensive work is precomputed, so the request path becomes a fast keyed lookup, with online fallbacks for missing, stale, or undersized results. Finally, stable run and item identifiers connect generation to impressions, plays, and follows.
Explain the offline decision: millions of request-time similarity searches would make latency and capacity unpredictable. Precomputation amortizes the cost and makes experiments reproducible. The tradeoff is freshness, so the design needs time-to-live grace periods, serve-time safety checks, and online fallbacks.
Clarify ownership: you built all data pipelines and most serving integration, and co-designed the retrieval/ranking contracts. This is the technical center of the presentation; be ready to go deeper in Q&A rather than adding every implementation detail here.
Transition: ‘The clean diagram hides the part that taught me the most: my first implementation did not work at production scale.’

[Sources]

name: pipeline-lesson
text: Lesson: at this scale, data grain is architecture—not an implementation detail.
textPreview: Lesson: at this scale, data grain is architecture—not an implementation detail.

text:
Timing: 13:20–15:45.
Tell this as a failure story, not a victory lap. ‘I did not have a data-engineering background. My first design was logically valid and looked fine on a development cohort, but it joined at too broad a grain. In production-scale validation it created a 23.4-billion-row intermediate, spilled roughly four terabytes locally, and timed out after four hours.’
Then show tenacity: inspect the query plan, isolate where cardinality multiplied, rewrite the join so bucket eligibility is part of the key, and verify output equivalence on a bounded cohort before scaling up. The fix was not a bigger warehouse; it was a better data model.
Reflection: you learned to write down grain and cardinality before writing SQL, estimate fan-out, and validate both correctness and cost. This converts lack of prior experience into evidence of learning speed.
Transition: ‘Performance failures were visible. Data-semantic failures were more dangerous because they could look like bad recommendations.’

[Sources]
- User-provided Recommendation Feeds technical guide: historical candidate fan-out measurement and bucket-aware join optimization.
[/Sources]

name: messy-lesson
text: Debug the data contract before tuning the model.
textPreview: Debug the data contract before tuning the model.

text:
Timing: 15:45–18:00.
Describe the environment neutrally: a fast-moving codebase with overlapping data sources, historical tables, current-state views, and multiple identifier domains. The challenge was not that the code was ‘bad’; it was that reasonable assumptions could silently select the wrong source.
Give one concrete debugging method: choose a single affected user and follow the recommendation from input signal to retrieved candidate, ranked item, stored feed, served response, and impression event. This showed whether the failure was retrieval, state, identity mapping, filtering, or UI exposure.
Then describe the durable fixes: document the grain and identifier contract, replace whole snapshots rather than only upserting incoming items, tag the actual serving source, and build validation queries and production metrics. This is a deployed-engineer pattern: make an ambiguous system observable before trying to optimize it.
Transition: ‘The third class of problems was product-semantic: creation behavior broke assumptions that work in a normal listening product.’

name: creation-after-label
text: true floor: users with no eligible, embeddable creation
textPreview: true floor: users with no eligible, embeddable creation

name: creation-rules
text: The final feed also required a visible anchor, owner-only private access, and rotation among strong creations to avoid repetition.
textPreview: The final feed also required a visible anchor, owner-only private access, and rotation among strong creations to avoid repetition.

text:
Timing: 18:00–20:30.
Explain the original logic: select one strong creation, then require an audio representation. If that one sample lacked the representation, the user received no seed—even if they had many other eligible creations. Historical analysis showed 47.12% of users were zeroed by this ordering. Filtering for eligible, embeddable creations first and sampling second reduced the zero-seed rate to the true floor of 7.91%.
Connect the bug to product semantics. Always choosing the single top creation would be repetitive, so the design rotates among strong creations. The anchor must appear in the shelf or the title is inexplicable. A user may see their own private or stylized work, while another user must never see it. Those rules make this more than a nearest-neighbor query.
Be explicit that the percentages are from a historical eligible cohort, not current MAU. This prevents an apparent inconsistency with the scale figures on slide 2.
Transition: ‘Once we had the system and semantics right, experiments—not opinion—decided what graduated.’

The personalized creator experiment asked whether matching people to creators would improve durable relationships; net follows rose 15%, with the launch summary marking the result statistically significant and guardrails flat. text:
Timing: 22:30–24:00.
Synthesize rather than repeat. The visible outputs are three feeds, but the engineering leverage is a reusable capability: feed behavior can be configured and experimented with; request-time serving is fast and resilient; outcomes are attributable; and the system has an owner who can diagnose it in production.
This is where you demonstrate prioritization. You could have built three independent pipelines faster in the first week, but a shared candidate contract, feed-specific assembly, and common serving path reduced long-term iteration cost. At the same time, you did not over-generalize the product semantics: each feed still has its own anchor, entity, and cold-start rules.
Transition: ‘The project changed how I approach ambiguous production problems.’

text:
Timing: 24:00–25:00, then Q&A.
Close by resolving the opening. ‘I started without a recommendation or data-engineering background. What I learned is that the model is only one part of a production recommendation system. The difficult work is aligning the product hypothesis, the data contract, the serving path, the experiment, and the operating model.’
State what you would do differently: map data grain and identifier domains in the first week; establish a metric tree and exposure definition before implementation; and design fallbacks, attribution, and health dashboards alongside the first prototype rather than after it.
Final line: ‘The part I am proudest of is not that I learned recommendation systems quickly. It is that I took an ambiguous, under-owned product problem and built the path from diagnosis to measurable production impact.’ Then stop. Let the interviewers ask the first question.
